name: Annapurna I Expedition
sub_region: Myagdi/Kaski border, Gandaki Province (north side via Miristi Khola; Annapurna Conservation Area)

difficulty.notes: 8,091 m, 10th highest mountain. Normal north-side route (French route and variants such as the Dutch Rib / German route); crux is the avalanche- and serac-exposed section between Camp 2 and Camp 3 below the 'Sickle', with 45-55 degree ramps above. Historically the deadliest 8,000er by summit-to-fatality ratio (~32% per 8000ers.com data); The Himalayan Database later recorded 476 summits and 73 deaths. Prior 6,000-7,000 m experience expected by operators. [s5][s6][s7][s8]

duration_days.notes: Commercial programmes typically fly or drive to Pokhara, drive to Dana (Kali Gandaki) and helicopter to Base Camp; alternatively drive Dana-Hunggung Khola (~2,900 m) and trek to Base Camp. Modern teams often climb fast and early in spring to reduce avalanche exposure, using heavy fixed rope, oxygen and helicopter support. [s3][s4][s9]

itinerary.notes: BC listed 4,130-4,400 m historically; 4,190 m in current commercial programmes. Puja at BC. [s3][s5]

itinerary.route: Acclimatisation and rotations: BC - Camp I (5,150 m) - Camp II (5,700 m) - BC
itinerary.notes: Camp I is mixed glacier terrain; Camp II is exposed and not suitable for long stays. Many clients rotate only to C1 and C2 to limit time in the C2-C3 avalanche zone. [s3][s6][s9]

itinerary.route: Summit window: BC - Camp II - Camp III (6,500 m) - Camp IV (7,400 m) - summit (8,091 m) - descend
itinerary.notes: Late-night summit start, summit typically 8-10 am, descend to C3/C2. Supplemental oxygen used by commercial teams. Camp altitudes vary by year: C3 ~6,400-6,600 m, C4 ~6,850-7,400 m. [s3][s5][s6]

best_seasons.notes: Commercial programmes start mid-March; teams aim to climb early in the season before warmer temperatures increase avalanche hazard. [s3][s9]

permits.name: Mountaineering royalty (Department of Tourism) - peaks above 8,000 m except Everest and Manaslu
permits.fee: Per foreign climber: USD 3,000 spring, USD 1,500 autumn, USD 750 winter/summer

permits.name: Garbage management deposit (Annapurna range, peaks above 8,001 m)
permits.fee: USD 3,000 per expedition, refundable on compliance

permits.name: Annapurna Conservation Area Permit (ACAP)
permits.fee: NPR 3,000 per foreign national (SAARC NPR 1,000), tax included

guide_requirements: Under the sixth amendment to the Mountaineering Regulations (effective for royalties from 1 Sept 2025), solo ascents of 8,000 m peaks are barred and every two members must be accompanied by at least one high-altitude worker or mountain guide. [s2][s11] Expedition teams must include a government-deputed liaison officer (Tourism Act). [s12]

flights: Helicopter Dana - Base Camp and return [s3]
drives: Optional drive Dana - Hunggung Khola (~2,900 m) then trek to BC [s4]
logistics.notes: Hotels in Kathmandu/Pokhara, lodge in Dana, ~1 month in tented Base Camp; helicopter resupply common. [s3]

highlights: First 8,000 m peak ever climbed (Herzog and Lachenal, 3 June 1950) [s13]
Remote north-side base camp above the Kali Gandaki [s3]
risks: Serac fall and avalanches between Camp 2 and Camp 3 (37 of 72 deaths to 2019 were avalanches) [s6][s7]
Limited acclimatisation on fast modern ascents; reliance on fixed rope and oxygen logistics [s9]

acclimatization.notes: Rotation period of roughly days 6-29 in the commercial programme. [s3]

unverified: Permit validity for 8,000 m expeditions: reported shortened from 75 to 55 days in the 2025 amendment (Kathmandu Post reported for Everest; scope for other 8,000ers not confirmed).

Whether TIMS/ACAP is charged separately to expedition members (TAAN states TIMS is not required for climbers holding mountaineering permits; ACAP applicability for expeditions not confirmed from an official expedition source).
Camp altitudes vary by year and operator (C3 6,300-6,600 m; C4 6,850-7,400 m).
